title: Question 6
stem:
A rectangular coil $PQRS$ of wire is free to rotate about its axis $XY$, as shown in Fig. 6.1.

{{figure:figure_6_1}}

Fig. 6.1 (not to scale)

The coil has length $QR$ of $5.4\text{ cm}$, width $PQ$ of $2.5\text{ cm}$ and has 190 turns of wire.
The plane of the coil is at an angle $\theta$ to a uniform magnetic field of flux density $5.2 \times 10^{-3}\text{ T}$.
The axis $XY$ of the coil is normal to the field.
The current in the coil is $1.2\text{ A}$.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the force on side $QR$ of the coil.
hints: Hint 1: Look at side QR in Fig. 6.1. Which length of wire is actually cutting across the magnetic field lines, and how many times does the current pass through that region?
Hint 2: Recall that the force on each single length of wire perpendicular to a uniform field scales with $B$, $I$ and $L$, then multiply by the total number of turns $N$ in the coil.
Hint 3: Convert QR = 5.4 cm to metres before substituting $B = 5.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}$, $I = 1.2 \text{ A}$, $L = 0.054 \text{ m}$ and $N = 190$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why side QR feels maximum force**
Side QR is parallel to the rotation axis XY and always perpendicular to the magnetic field direction. That means $\sin 90^{\circ} = 1$, so you get the full $BIL$ force on that side.

Step 2: **Include all 190 turns**
One turn would feel $BIL$. The coil has $N = 190$ identical turns carrying the same current, so the total force adds up: $$F = NBIL$$

Step 3: **Substitute with SI units**
Use $L_{QR} = 5.4 \text{ cm} = 0.054 \text{ m}$: $$F = 190 \times (5.2 \times 10^{-3}) \times 1.2 \times 0.054$$ $$F \approx 6.4 \times 10^{-2} \text{ N} = 0.064 \text{ N}$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text:
Use your answer in (a)(i) to show that the torque $\tau$ on the coil is given by

$$\tau = 1.6 \times 10^{-3} \cos \theta \text{ N m}.$$

markscheme_points.text: torque = force $\times$ perpendicular distance between forces

hints: Hint 1: From the END VIEW, focus on the two equal and opposite forces on PS (up) and QR (down). What is the separation between their lines of action measured perpendicular to the forces?
Hint 2: Use $\text{torque} = \text{force} \times \text{perpendicular separation}$, where the separation involves the coil width PQ = 0.025 m projected by $\cos\theta$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **A couple produces the torque**
The forces on PS and QR are equal in size, opposite in direction and offset from the axis. Together they form a couple, so: $$\tau = F \times \text{perpendicular distance between the forces}$$

Step 2: **Find the perpendicular distance**
The coil width is $PQ = 2.5 \text{ cm} = 0.025 \text{ m}$. From the end view geometry, the horizontal lever arm between the two vertical forces is $PQ \cos\theta$. Hence: $$\tau = 0.064 \times 0.025 \cos\theta$$ $$\tau = 1.6 \times 10^{-3} \cos\theta \text{ N m}$$ When $\theta = 0$ the separation is largest, so torque is maximum.

parts.label: (a)(iii)

markscheme_points.text: one complete cycle of a sinusoidal curve between 0 and 360°
$\tau$ axis labelled to show maximum and minimum torques at $\pm 1.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N m}$
maximum at 0 and 360° and minimum at 180° (or vice versa), with torque shown as zero at 90° and 270°

hints: Hint 1: Think about the shape of $y = \cos\theta$ from $0^{\circ}$ to $360^{\circ}$. Where does it start, where does it cross zero, and where does it go negative?
Hint 2: Work out the numerical values of $\tau$ at $\theta = 0^{\circ}, 90^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}, 270^{\circ}, 360^{\circ}$ using $1.6 \times 10^{-3}\cos\theta$.
Hint 3: Check how to label the vertical axis $\tau / 10^{-3} \text{ N m}$ so that +1.6 is the top peak and -1.6 is the bottom trough.
parts.proper_answer: Cosine curve from 0 to $360^{\circ}$ with max $+1.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N m}$ at $0^{\circ}$ and $360^{\circ}$, zero at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$, min $-1.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N m}$ at $180^{\circ}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise the cosine shape**
Since $\tau \propto \cos\theta$, you sketch one full cosine wave. Start high at $\theta = 0$, fall to zero at $90^{\circ}$, go negative to a trough at $180^{\circ}$, return to zero at $270^{\circ}$ and back to max at $360^{\circ}$.

Step 2: **Add the correct scale**
Maximum magnitude is $1.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N m}$. On an axis labelled $\tau / 10^{-3} \text{ N m}$, mark +1.6 at the peaks ($0^{\circ}$, $360^{\circ}$) and -1.6 at the trough ($180^{\circ}$).

Step 3: **Check zero crossings**
Torque is zero when the coil plane is perpendicular to the field ($\cos 90^{\circ} = \cos 270^{\circ} = 0$). Make sure your smooth sinusoidal curve passes exactly through zero at $90^{\circ}$ and $270^{\circ}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The coil is now replaced by an identical coil wound on a ferrous core.

Suggest, with a reason, how the torque on this coil compares with the torque on the original coil.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a ferrous (iron) core does to magnetic field lines passing through a coil - does it concentrate them or spread them out?
Hint 2: Link the change in effective $B$ inside the coil to the formulas $F = NBIL$ and $\tau = NBIA\cos\theta$ to decide what happens to the amplitude of the graph in (a)(iii).
parts.proper_answer: Torque increases in amplitude because the ferrous core concentrates the field and increases the effective magnetic flux density $B$ acting on the coil.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Effect of the iron core on the field**
A ferrous core is easily magnetised and concentrates magnetic flux lines. For the same external magnets, the flux density $B$ through the coil becomes much larger.

Step 2: **Effect on torque**
Both force and torque are directly proportional to $B$: $$F = NBIL, \quad \tau = NBIA\cos\theta$$ So larger $B$ gives larger forces on PS and QR and a larger peak torque. The shape $\cos\theta$ stays the same but the amplitude increases.
